BOOK I / AN ARTIST-RESEARCH ATLAS

Listen first.
Then name.

This is a book about a real practice with two instruments: Amastacia, the drone, and Ankora, the pulse. Its drawings are conceptual, not disguised measurements. Its marks are provisional and their meaning must be earned in sound. Enter through any plate or read straight through.

PROLOGUE01 / 31
FIELD OBSERVATION / 01

The sound came first.

Before there was an atlas, there was a breath held against a hollow column of agave. A note gathered in the room. Not a perfect tone, not an electronic constant, but a living sound with an edge, a grain, and the audible effort of its making.

A drum entered. One strike divided the sound into a before and an after. Another strike made the interval imaginable. With the third, the ear could begin waiting for the fourth. Nothing supernatural had occurred. Something stranger had: a mind had begun building time around an expectation.

KLAAT began in this encounter between a sound that continues and a gesture that interrupts. Its two principal instruments are Amastacia, an agave didgeridoo pitched in C-sharp, and Ankora, an elk-hide frame drum. Their materials are ancient in kind, but their relationship here is particular: the pressure of a breath, the weight of a hand, the body of a room, and the willingness to remain with a sound long enough for it to change.

This book is an attempt to learn the shape of what is happening without pretending to possess its final explanation.

KLAAT / AN ATLAS OF RELATION 01
PROLOGUE02 / 31
FIELD OBSERVATION / 02

A practice, not a doctrine.

There is no single frequency hidden inside KLAAT that unlocks the nervous system. There is no universal tempo that commands trance. There is no evidence that a listener who feels vibration has experienced one particular biological event. The instrument does not become more extraordinary when we give it powers it cannot be shown to have.

Yet these exclusions do not leave us with a small art. They leave the real mystery unobstructed. Sound reaches us through pressure, reflection, memory, anticipation, movement, and attention. A stable drone is not static. Repetition is not identical experience repeated. The same acoustic event can belong to different stories in different bodies and different rooms.

The pages that follow describe an emergent discipline: a way of making, noticing, naming, testing, and transmitting relationships between sound and experience. The field remains open. Its grammar is provisional; its symbols are invented here and must earn their use in performance; its research claims can be revised by evidence.

The system must grow from the music. The music owes the system nothing.

KLAAT / AN ATLAS OF RELATION 02
PLATE 01 / SCHEMATIC03 / 31

I / THE HELD FIELD

A sustained pitch is not a stationary event. Breath, spectral movement and articulation continually remake it.

KLAAT / ARCHAEOSONIC ATLAS 03
FIELD I04 / 31
FIELD OBSERVATION / 04

A line that refuses to be still.

Amastacia can occupy a single tonal center while producing a succession of changing internal events. The fundamental gives the listener something to return to. Above and around it, harmonics gather and recede, the vocal tract reshapes the sound, breath alters its envelope, roughness appears, and the human edge of the instrument remains audible.

A line on paper usually represents duration as an unbroken stroke. It cannot show how much activity may take place inside that continuity. The first task of KLAAT notation is therefore to resist the dead straight line. A held sound should appear held, but never inert.

The drone can be heard as a floor beneath other events, yet it may also become the most active participant. A shift in the overtone structure can feel like movement even when the drum has stopped. A brief roughened articulation can sharpen the air without changing the musical tempo. The breath itself makes interruptions too fine to count as conventional beats.

C-sharp names the pitch of this particular instrument. It is a condition of KLAAT's sound, not a claim about the biological privilege of that note. Its meaning was acquired through encounter, not assigned by a frequency chart.

KLAAT / AN ATLAS OF RELATION 04
FIELD I05 / 31
FIELD OBSERVATION / 05

The difference between presence and stillness.

Listening to a continuous sound changes what the ear treats as new. At first, the drone announces itself as an object: a pitch, a volume, a timbre. With time, it becomes a condition. The listener begins to notice what occurs within it: tiny fluctuations, accents from the mouth, the interaction between tones, the way a room emphasizes one part and swallows another.

The shift is not guaranteed, and there is no reason to expect everyone to experience it. Some listeners become absorbed; others grow restless. That difference belongs inside our account, not outside it.

KLAAT treats continuity as something composed with, rather than a state one enters on command. The performer can sustain the sound and still leave enough openness for unexpected events. The hand does not have to solve the breath. The breath does not have to mirror the hand.

An anchor is not an instruction to remain in place. It is what makes departure legible.

KLAAT / AN ATLAS OF RELATION 05
PLATE 02 / SCHEMATIC06 / 31

II / THE FIRST DIVISION

The strike is not simply a sound; it offers the ear a point from which to measure another arrival.

KLAAT / ARCHAEOSONIC ATLAS 06
FIELD II07 / 31
FIELD OBSERVATION / 07

The first strike makes a past.

Ankora is an elk-hide frame drum. Its attack is brief when compared with the continuous field surrounding it, but the consequences endure. One strike can become an event. Two can become an interval. Repetition encourages the listener to form a prediction about what comes next.

A steady pulse is not a command. It is an agreement the ear may accept. Once learned, even an omitted strike can become meaningful; absence is heard against an expectation. The performer does not always have to add sound to create an event.

This is one of KLAAT's central distinctions: pace, density, accent and force are not interchangeable. The number of anchor beats per minute may remain unchanged while smaller strokes accumulate between them. A piece may feel more crowded without getting faster. It may become more urgent through timbre instead of volume.

A rhythm is therefore better understood as a living hierarchy than as one number printed beside a metronome.

KLAAT / AN ATLAS OF RELATION 07
FIELD II08 / 31
FIELD OBSERVATION / 08

A recoverable path.

The ear can tolerate complexity differently when a recurring reference remains available. An attack that returns at a recognizable interval gives the listener a way through a dense surface. Additional accents can cross the center of that pattern. They can compete with it, conceal it, or illuminate it after a pause.

The relationship is not universally soothing or universally activating. Context matters: sound level, personal preference, expectation, duration, room acoustics, and what the listener is doing. KLAAT is interested in the tension between a recognizable ground and the instability that can grow around it.

The recorded pulse of one early performance was approximately 137 beats per minute. That is useful as a calibration reference for that recording. It is not an optimal tempo for humanity, and it should never become a law of the practice.

The beat returns. What returns with it may be changed.

KLAAT / AN ATLAS OF RELATION 08
PLATE 03 / SCHEMATIC09 / 31

III / THE DISTRIBUTED ROOM

A venue is not one acoustic condition. The same sound may bloom or disappear a few steps away.

KLAAT / ARCHAEOSONIC ATLAS 09
FIELD III10 / 31
FIELD OBSERVATION / 10

The room does not listen evenly.

A drone enters a room and is no longer only the performer's sound. Walls reflect it; dimensions favor some frequency regions and weaken others; furniture absorbs or scatters energy; a floor or chair may move. What one listener hears near a corner is not identical to what another hears closer to the center.

This is a measurable fact of acoustics, and one of the most fertile artistic conditions of KLAAT. A room is not a passive container. Its shape participates in the performance without intention. To move through it is to move through different versions of the same source.

The diagram opposite is conceptual, not a survey of an actual venue. Pale contours indicate regions of relative acoustic difference; they do not claim that a particular pressure field has been measured. A future version of this atlas can place real microphone positions, sound-pressure maps and instrument recordings alongside the artistic plates.

The room can be called an instrument in poetry. In science, it is better called a distributed acoustic system. KLAAT needs room for both descriptions, provided they are not mistaken for each other.

KLAAT / AN ATLAS OF RELATION 10
FIELD III11 / 31
FIELD OBSERVATION / 11

The small speaker problem.

There is another room inside each recording: the playback system. A phone may preserve the identity of a low note through its upper harmonics while failing to reproduce much of its low-frequency pressure. The melody of an instrument can survive in miniature when its physical weight does not.

This raises a practical question for any music built around breath, drum and resonance. What must survive when the bass disappears? It may be the rhythm of the air itself. It may be the roughness, a vocal inflection, a recognizable spacing of attacks, the slow rise of a texture, the way one event reveals another.

KLAAT should be made for the particular room in which it happens, then studied again when carried elsewhere. No device is a transparent window. Translation is part of the work.

There is no single KLAAT experience. There are encounters made under particular conditions.

KLAAT / AN ATLAS OF RELATION 11
PLATE 04 / SCHEMATIC12 / 31

IV / THE BODY AS WITNESS

The body reports an experience. Its report is meaningful, but it does not by itself identify a mechanism.

KLAAT / ARCHAEOSONIC ATLAS 12
FIELD IV13 / 31
FIELD OBSERVATION / 13

Where did the sound go?

A listener may point to the chest, the floor, the throat, or an apparently moving line through the body. Such descriptions deserve attention. They are data about lived experience. They are not, by themselves, a map of the physical route vibration traveled.

Airborne sound reaches the ear. Some environments also transmit mechanical vibration through surfaces in contact with the body. Perception integrates hearing, touch, expectation, posture and memory. The same language of 'feeling the sound' can refer to different combinations of these processes.

KLAAT refuses two temptations here. The first is to dismiss sensation because it cannot immediately be instrumented. The second is to proclaim a hidden physiology every time a sensation feels vivid. A stronger practice records what occurred, asks what might explain it, and leaves room for an experience that exceeds its current account.

When people describe intensity, warmth, pressure, movement or altered attention, we will listen closely. We will not quietly translate those words into a diagnosis, a brainwave, or evidence of healing.

KLAAT / AN ATLAS OF RELATION 13
FIELD IV14 / 31
FIELD OBSERVATION / 14

The listener completes nothing.

There is a phrase we should avoid: that the listener completes the composition. It makes a seductive claim about artistic wholeness that KLAAT does not need. The sound is already an event. The listener does not finish it; the listener lives through a particular version of it.

Some will hear cycles that were not deliberately composed. Some will lose count. Some will move. Some will remain still. A striking moment for one listener may pass almost unnoticed by another, even at the same point in the performance.

The task of documentation is not to eliminate these differences, but to make them legible. We can ask listeners what they noticed before telling them what they were supposed to hear. We can compare their accounts with the actual recording. We can discover what the performer intended and what the room allowed.

An experience is evidence of an experience. A mechanism requires another kind of evidence.

KLAAT / AN ATLAS OF RELATION 14
PLATE 05 / SCHEMATIC15 / 31

V / THE UNEQUAL CLOCKS

Anchor pulse, surface density and perceived intensity can move independently.

KLAAT / ARCHAEOSONIC ATLAS 15
FIELD V16 / 31
FIELD OBSERVATION / 16

More events do not make faster time.

A drum can remain at the same underlying pace while the space between its main strikes fills with smaller sounds. The listener may feel acceleration. Yet the organizing pulse has not moved. We need a vocabulary able to describe this without reducing every increase in energy to a change in tempo.

KLAAT calls the persistent reference the anchor and the changing frequency of audible attacks the density. Accent describes which events carry weight. Grain describes the quality of an attack or the texture within the sustained sound. These are working terms, not discoveries of new universal laws.

Duration allows these dimensions to exchange importance. A sparse pattern may be heard as steady until a nearly inaudible accent redefines its grouping. A cluster of strikes can become a new background. Silence between attacks may gain more force once the listener has learned a richer expectation.

The atlas records relationships rather than insisting that any one configuration must produce a prescribed state.

KLAAT / AN ATLAS OF RELATION 16
FIELD V17 / 31
FIELD OBSERVATION / 17

The chapter no one composed.

Long performances contain a peculiar form of storytelling: listeners sometimes report beginnings, passages and returns the performer never marked. These private chapters may be encouraged by repeated motifs, changing textures, fatigue, attention, or the act of remembering the work afterward.

If a passage feels as though it lasted for ten minutes, that does not tell us its measured duration. If a return feels inevitable, that does not prove it was planned. Such differences are not errors to correct. They are part of how time becomes experienced rather than counted.

KLAAT should preserve the distinction between the event clock, the performer's clock and the listener's clock. None can substitute for the others. Their divergences are among the most interesting things the music can reveal.

The clock counts. The mind organizes. The body endures. Their stories sometimes meet.

KLAAT / AN ATLAS OF RELATION 17
PLATE 06 / SCHEMATIC18 / 31

VI / MARKS FOR A LIVING SOUND

A provisional notation that can record a relationship without claiming to explain everything heard.

KLAAT / ARCHAEOSONIC ATLAS 18
FIELD VI19 / 31
FIELD OBSERVATION / 19

The need for marks.

An instrument can be learned by imitation. A practice begins to travel when its recurring distinctions can also be named. The words do not replace the sound. They give a musician something to remember, alter, question and teach.

We begin with four primitive marks. The FIELD denotes an audible continuity. The STRIKE marks a discrete attack. The DRIFT shows that a recurring relationship has changed without vanishing. The RETURN points to a recognizable condition appearing again after departure. None is sacred. None means 'trance.' Their value is practical: can they help a player remember what occurred, or discover a new way of playing?

A field can contain several drifts. A strike can occur without becoming an anchor. A return can be delayed, partial or disputed. Such distinctions matter more than ornamental complexity. If a sign never helps us hear, perform, or think, it should be discarded.

We are not inventing a counterfeit antiquity. These marks are contemporary instruments of attention, made openly and revised through use.

KLAAT / AN ATLAS OF RELATION 19
FIELD VI20 / 31
FIELD OBSERVATION / 20

A grammar is not a script.

A script tells a performer what happens next. A grammar describes how elements may relate. The difference is the difference between memorizing a sentence and learning to speak.

The earliest KLAAT studies might use plain operations: sustain a field while varying its grain; establish an anchor without filling every subdivision; exchange strong and weak accents; let an established pattern lose its certainty; bring back a former condition without reproducing its first appearance.

These operations can be combined. The outcome should not be guaranteed. The point of the notation is to sharpen awareness, not to standardize surprise.

A mature vocabulary would grow through recordings, performance notes, experiments and, eventually, teaching. Its names would be assigned to reproducible musical relationships, not to unverified claims about what every listener must feel.

The moment the notation becomes more important than listening, it has failed.

KLAAT / AN ATLAS OF RELATION 20
PLATE 07 / SCHEMATIC21 / 31

VII / A LANGUAGE CAN BE TAUGHT

Repetition, oral encoding, responsive judgment and learned cues are technical resources for study, not traditions to claim as our own.

KLAAT / ARCHAEOSONIC ATLAS 21
FIELD VII22 / 31
FIELD OBSERVATION / 22

What the drum traditions teach.

The investigation of KLAAT eventually led outward, toward musicians who have long developed structured relationships between rhythm, apprenticeship, context and belief. What emerged was not a universal secret beat. It was a family of very different practices, each situated in its own history.

Research on Newar dhimay pedagogy describes spoken stroke syllables and patterned transformations performed forward, backward and in mirrored forms. Work on Kham-Magar ritual speech describes how learned formulas can support long improvisational utterance. Korean jangdan shows how a named rhythmic cycle can hold internal organization far richer than a metronome number. These are different cultural systems, not pieces of one hidden global method.

The transferable insight is not a repertoire we can simply claim. It is a developmental principle: sound becomes generative when distinctions are learned so deeply that they can be recombined with judgment. To borrow that principle honestly means naming the traditions, studying their contexts and composing our own material.

KLAAT will not describe itself as an inherited Indigenous lineage, or rename a borrowed ceremonial pattern as its own discovery.

KLAAT / AN ATLAS OF RELATION 22
FIELD VII23 / 31
FIELD OBSERVATION / 23

The lesson of the callback.

Michael Harner's modern Core Shamanism offers a very different example. Its characteristic journey-drumming format employs an extended steady rhythmic passage and a conspicuous closing or return cue. The cue acquires meaning partly because listeners learn what it is meant to announce. This is not proof that a given beat rate induces a universal neurological state.

For KLAAT, the interesting phenomenon is learned musical information. A sound can function as a signal once it belongs to a shared practice. A particular return, omission or change in grain might later become recognizable to experienced participants without needing spoken instruction every time.

The existence of a cue does not require copying Harner's method. We can develop original sonic relationships, observe whether anyone actually recognizes them, and revise the language when the evidence disagrees.

The goal is not to reproduce someone else's ceremonies. It is to understand how a musical system becomes coherent and transmissible while remaining accountable to the cultures and people from whom we have learned.

KLAAT / AN ATLAS OF RELATION 23
PLATE 08 / SCHEMATIC24 / 31

VIII / THE FORM STAYS OPEN

The architecture is descriptive. The performance remains free to find, refuse or alter it.

KLAAT / ARCHAEOSONIC ATLAS 24
FIELD VIII25 / 31
FIELD OBSERVATION / 25

Four names, no commandments.

Earlier KLAAT work used four names: Ground Anchor, Threshold Gate, Rising Pulse and Return Path. They remain useful when a performance can genuinely be heard through that lens. One may establish a regularity; one may unsettle it; one may thicken the pulse; one may reveal an earlier condition again.

But these are not required movements, universal psychological stages, or a promise about listener experience. A performance may begin in density. It may refuse the gate. It may never return. A valuable notation must be capable of documenting what actually happened, including the event that defeats its categories.

Improvisation is not the absence of discipline. It is the ability to remain responsive while carrying a body of practiced technique. Breath and hand may enter into temporary agreement, then separate. Density may emerge from listening rather than a predetermined curve.

The living rule is simple and difficult: preserve a capacity to notice. Do not let the desire for a named structure prevent the music from contradicting it.

KLAAT / AN ATLAS OF RELATION 25
FIELD VIII26 / 31
FIELD OBSERVATION / 26

The performer is not the audience.

There are moments when playing becomes nearly automatic: breathing continues, the hand moves, and choices appear less like decisions than like attention taking shape. Such states can be artistically significant without proving that the listener is having the same experience.

The performer has access to muscle, breath pressure, effort, technical challenge and intention. The listener has access to an acoustic event filtered through a location, a body and a history. Their experiences can intersect, but they cannot be substituted for one another.

We can document both. After an uninterrupted performance, the player can describe moments of freedom, strain, transition and surprise. A listener can describe the recording without being told the intended arc. The distance between those accounts might reveal more than a score that claims to predict them.

A discipline grows stronger by allowing its maker to be surprised by the evidence.

KLAAT / AN ATLAS OF RELATION 26
PLATE 09 / SCHEMATIC27 / 31

IX / WHAT THE ATLAS CAN KNOW

A drawing may illuminate an idea. It is not automatically an instrument reading.

KLAAT / ARCHAEOSONIC ATLAS 27
FIELD IX28 / 31
FIELD OBSERVATION / 28

Four kinds of statement.

KLAAT can remain artistically strange while being exact about the status of its claims. An OBSERVATION records an event we witnessed or heard. A MEASUREMENT reports a quantity gathered by an instrument or procedure. An INFERENCE offers a possible explanation. A FICTION or METAPHOR makes an image without claiming it is a mechanism.

Those categories should accompany the atlas invisibly enough not to burden every page, but clearly enough that a reader can always find the boundary. A ring drawn around a drum stroke may represent an audible expansion. Unless calibrated to actual audio, it is not a pressure map. A field of dots may represent increasing attack density. Unless tied to timestamps, it is not a transcription.

The scientific manuscript that preceded this atlas established substantial literature-led foundations. It did not establish that KLAAT itself reliably induces trance, entrains a brain, treats disease or causes particular physiological changes. Those questions require recordings, measurements and listener studies.

The first responsibility of this atlas is not to resolve the mystery. It is to keep the mystery honest.

KLAAT / AN ATLAS OF RELATION 28
FIELD IX29 / 31
FIELD OBSERVATION / 29

The experiment begins after the music.

A performance should first be allowed to exist on its own terms. Then it can become an object of study. We can record uninterrupted sessions and mark the events that felt important without editing the work to fit a favored theory. We can invite listeners to describe what they heard before providing our vocabulary. We can compare accounts across rooms and playback systems.

The earliest questions are modest and consequential. Can a listener identify a stable pulse under growing density? Do independently heard transitions align with the performer's intended changes? Which elements of KLAAT survive small speakers? Does repeated listening produce consistent new observations, or merely confidence in familiar descriptions?

The answers may disappoint a theory and deepen the art. That is a result worth having. The purpose of inquiry is not to announce KLAAT's power but to discover what its actual materials can support.

Let the sound remain free to contradict the page.

KLAAT / AN ATLAS OF RELATION 29
PLATE 10 / SCHEMATIC30 / 31

X / AN UNFINISHED RETURN

A return is not necessarily a resolution. The field may remain after the final strike.

KLAAT / ARCHAEOSONIC ATLAS 30
CODA31 / 31
FIELD OBSERVATION / 31

The work remains open.

The final strike ends before the room becomes silent. Some part of it may continue as reverberation. Some part persists as a remembered interval. The drone may fall away, but the listener can still anticipate another sound that will not arrive.

KLAAT is a practice of attending to such relationships: what continues, what interrupts, what is learned, what changes under repetition, and what remains unknown when the measurable event has ended.

This atlas is not the definitive vocabulary of those relationships. It is the first careful arrangement of marks, statements and questions around them. The names may change. The diagrams may become more exact. The body of recordings will grow. Future participants may hear structures that its maker never intended.

A discipline is not made enduring by declaring itself complete. It becomes real through repeated use, honest revision and work strong enough to invite another person into the inquiry.

The sound came first. It should always be permitted the last word.

KLAAT / AN ATLAS OF RELATION 31
AN UNFINISHED RETURN

The sound came first.
It keeps the last word.

The atlas is a completed first volume, not a closed doctrine. Future recordings, listening studies and musical practice may alter its language. Its scientific companion preserves the evidence, citations and unfinished questions behind the work.
